content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe the structure of simple covalent molecules
Explain the properties of simple covalent substances
Distinguish between intermolecular forces and covalent bonds
Explain why simple covalent substances have low melting and boiling points

Simple covalent molecules contain a small, fixed number of atoms held together by strong covalent bonds. Understanding the forces between molecules (not just within them) is key to explaining their properties.
(also called simple covalent substances) consist of small molecules.
Small molecules with a fixed number of atoms
H₂, O₂, H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, NH₃
[DIAGRAM: Simple molecules showing strong bonds within molecules and weak forces between them]
Properties depend mainly on intermolecular forces, NOT covalent bonds.
are weak attractions between molecules. They are much weaker than covalent bonds.
Van der Waals forces (present in all molecules)
For GCSE, you mainly need to know that intermolecular forces are weak compared to covalent bonds.
Weak intermolecular forces easy to overcome
Little energy needed to separate molecules
Simple covalent substances have low melting and boiling points because:
Little energy is needed to overcome these weak forces
The covalent bonds do NOT break when a substance melts or boils
Only the intermolecular forces are overcome
Breaking molecules = breaking covalent bonds (does NOT happen during melting/boiling)
Larger molecules = Stronger intermolecular forces = Higher boiling points
As molecules get larger, there are more electrons and more surface area for intermolecular forces to act on.
Why Simple Covalent Substances Don't Conduct
Simple covalent substances do not conduct electricity because:
No delocalised electrons (all electrons are used in bonding)
Even when melted, simple covalent substances don't conduct - they just become liquids of neutral molecules.
States of Matter at Room Temperature
Many simple covalent substances are gases at room temperature:
Water has higher melting and boiling points than expected because of
- a particularly strong type of intermolecular force.
Without hydrogen bonding, water would boil at about -80°C
Hydrogen bonding makes water liquid at room temperature
This is essential for life on Earth
Always specify that INTERMOLECULAR forces are weak, not covalent bonds
When explaining low melting points, say "weak intermolecular forces"
Do NOT say "weak covalent bonds" - covalent bonds are strong!
Saying simple covalent substances have weak covalent bonds
Covalent bonds are strong; it's the intermolecular forces that are weak
Saying covalent bonds break when a substance boils
Only intermolecular forces are overcome; molecules stay intact
Thinking all simple covalent substances are gases
Some are liquids (water, bromine) or solids (iodine, sulfur)
